key_insight: STEM replaces the FFN up-projection with a static, token-indexed embedding lookup while keeping gating and down-projection dense, enabling much larger parametric capacity without per-token routing or proportional compute. This removes runtime routing overhead and permits asynchronous CPU offload for more stable, scalable training.
problem_solved: Solves the training instability, load-balancing, routing latency, and communication overhead that hamper fine-grained sparse/mixture approaches, while decoupling model capacity from per-token compute cost.
method: Use a layer-local, token-indexed embedding lookup to supply the FFN up-projection instead of a dense matmul or dynamic router.
Keep the gating mechanism and the FFN down-projection dense to preserve expressivity and stability.
Eliminate runtime routing and enable asynchronous CPU offload/prefetch of embeddings to reduce peak memory and cross-device communication.
impact: Practitioners can scale transformer parameter counts with lower per-token compute and simpler runtimes, improving throughput, stability, and deployability (especially when leveraging CPU memory for large embeddings). This approach lowers engineering overhead compared with dynamic sparse routing.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: standard FFN / MoE with routing vs. STEM's FFN using token-indexed embedding lookup (highlight removed routing).
Pipeline illustration: asynchronous CPU embedding prefetch → local layer lookup → dense gate & down-projection (showing reduced communication).
Bar chart: effective parameter capacity vs per-token compute comparing dense, MoE, and STEM.
Icon set: stability (shield), low-latency/throughput (speedometer), memory offload (CPU chip + arrows), and simpler runtime (gear wrench).
paper_title: STEM: Scaling Transformers with Embedding Modules
paper_authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan, Sheng Cao, Harry Dong, Changsheng Zhao, Attiano Purpura-Pontoniere
